questions.q: What kind of scenario is Brennick Retail Holdings in this case study?
options: A fictional, illustrative scenario composited to show a real pattern, not an actual reported company or incident
A real, publicly reported company whose name has been anonymized
A hypothetical that never actually happens in real organizations
A direct quote from a published industry case study
questions.explain: Brennick Retail Holdings is explicitly fictional and illustrative, used to walk through the mechanism Chapter 2 warned about without presenting it as a real, reported incident.

questions.q: What was the key flaw in how Brennick's multi-cloud policy was adopted?
options: It applied to only one workload instead of the whole estate
It was adopted as a blanket architectural rule for every workload, with no per-workload cost model evaluating the tradeoff
It required too much documentation before any system could be built
It was based on a thorough cost-benefit analysis that simply turned out to be wrong
questions.explain: The policy was adopted as a universal principle rather than a decision evaluated per workload, which is exactly what Lesson 8 warns against.

questions.q: Which cost, specifically, grew because Brennick replicated data between Azure and AWS to give each cloud's deployment a local copy?
options: Licensing costs for the container registry
Help desk ticket volume
Recurring cross-cloud egress fees, which became one of the largest line items on the infrastructure budget
The cost of the animated logo video on the company website
questions.explain: Unmodeled, recurring egress cost from maintaining local copies in both clouds ended up dwarfing the compute cost it was supporting.

questions.q: What did most of Brennick's actual workloads -- internal reporting tools, low-traffic microsites, an HR portal -- have in common regarding the multi-cloud policy?
options: They were all exempted from the policy from the start
They were the primary reason the policy was created
They required multi-cloud for regulatory reasons
They had no real multi-cloud requirement at all, yet paid the full duplicated-tooling and duplicated-skill cost anyway
questions.explain: The majority of workloads had no genuine need for multi-cloud resilience, but the blanket policy didn't distinguish between workloads, so they paid the full cost anyway.

questions.q: What would Lesson 8's actual recommendation have changed about Brennick's outcome?
options: It would have banned multi-cloud architecture entirely across the company
It would have required every workload to run on three clouds instead of two
It would have left most workloads on one cloud by default, reserving deliberate multi-cloud duplication for the small number with a specific, costed justification
It would have eliminated the need for any cost model at all
questions.explain: Evaluating lock-in risk per workload, as Lesson 8 recommends, would have kept most of the estate on one cloud while reserving multi-cloud for workloads where the benefit was real and modeled.
